articles.title: School headscarf ban sparks rare protests in Azerbaijan and row with Turkey
articles.summary: Protests have taken place over the rules which have seen pupils wearing hijabs turned away from schools.
body: These schoolgirls were not allowed to enter classes because of their headscarves
"You are telling me, I can't come to school?" says a teenage girl in a navy blue Islamic headscarf, captured on video challenging a staff member at the entrance to her school.
The footage has been shared widely on social media, and shows a group of girls in hijabs standing behind her applauding as she continues: "Why should I have to give up my religion?"

Last Monday the education ministry in Azerbaijan began enforcing new uniform rules, turning away female pupils wearing hijabs. Protests began outside state schools in the capital, Baku, and in several southern districts including Masally and Jalilabad.
Protests are rare in this oil- and gas-producing country of 10.5 million people.
Azerbaijan is constitutionally secular and the government strongly enforces that.
President Ilham Aliyev has been in power since 2003 and has little tolerance for dissent. Opposition politicians and many independent journalists are in jail.
Azerbaijan is pulled between two neighbours, Turkey and Iran. Azerbaijanis belong to a Turkic group of nations, speaking a language close to Turkish, and Turkey is its closest ally.
But like Iran to the south, Azerbaijan is mainly Shia - over 60% of its people identify as Shia Muslims, while most Turks are Sunni.
The interior ministry said it had detained 37 people on Monday who tried to obstruct the rules and "grossly violate public order".
Videos have circulated of protests taking place in and around the capital Baku

The rules, approved on 21 September, ban clothing which contradict "the principle of secularism in education" in state schools. They do not mention the hijab. Similar guidelines were extended to teachers on 6 October.
In one video, pupils outside School No. 69 in Balakhany, outside Baku, hold a banner reading: "The hijab does not prevent anyone from getting an education."
Shahiza Huseynova, a mother who was protesting outside a school in the Mashtaga district of the capital, was detained on Tuesday.

In an interview with Meydan TV, an independent Azerbaijani-language channel based in Germany, Huseynova's husband Agha said she had been given a warning: "Either you take off your child's hijab and send them to school, or you go to prison."
An example shared by the Azerbaijani government of an acceptable school uniform under the new rules

Friends have also lost contact with Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who on Tuesday launched an online platform called "Let Leyli Go to School". It offers free lessons from volunteer teachers to pupils barred from class.
According to a friend, Huseynov left his home in Baku with unidentified men at about 16:00 on Wednesday, and his phone has been switched off ever since.
The authorities have not commented, but friends believe he has been detained. On Thursday, the platform's Instagram page could not be accessed.
Since the protests began, users have reported problems accessing Instagram and TikTok without a virtual private network (VPN).
Most of the protests have been in religiously conservative neighbourhoods in Baku's outlying settlements and in southern districts near the 765km (475-mile) border with Iran.
The authorities have long been wary of religious influence from Iran, where more ethnic Azerbaijanis live than in Azerbaijan itself.
On the night of 13 October, Azerbaijan's State Service for Special Communications and Information Security said a "foreign hacker group" had attacked more than 100 state websites.
A pro-Iranian group calling itself the 313 Team (Cyber Islamic Resistance) claimed responsibility.
Azerbaijani officials have defended the rules. One MP, Nigar Arpadarai, told the 1news.az website that children did not choose to wear the hijab themselves but were influenced by their families.
"A child has no freedom to choose a religion. This is a conscious prerogative of adults," she said.
Azerbaijan pardons Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire
Azerbaijan and Armenia sign peace pledge at White House summit with Trump
The row has now spilled over into Turkey, Baku's closest ally, which provided vital support during Azerbaijan's 2020 war with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh.
The two countries call themselves "one nation, two states".
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, a devout Muslim, has spoken of creating a "pious generation".
His chief adviser, Oktay Saral, has called the Azerbaijani restrictions "unacceptable" and urged Baku to "reverse this mistake".
"A headscarf is not an obstacle; it is a requirement of one's faith!" Saral wrote on X.
Several MPs from Turkey's governing AK Party joined in.

Small demonstrations were held outside Azerbaijan's embassy in Ankara, organised by Köklü Değişim, an Islamist movement linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, and outside its consulate in Istanbul, organised by conservative Islamist group Özgür-Der.

President Aliyev's New Azerbaijan Party accused Turkish officials of an "openly defamatory" information campaign and of "baseless accusations", warning that Oktay Saral's comments risked harming ties, and cautioned against interference in Azerbaijan's internal affairs.
Earlier this month, Ilham Aliyev himself said no one should "stick their noses into our way of life".

Behind the dispute there may lie another source of friction. Turkish protesters have linked the headscarf rules to Azerbaijan's close ties with Israel, which sells weapons to Baku and buys Azerbaijani oil.
Turkey's relations with Israel have collapsed over Gaza, but Azerbaijan has tried to maintain relationships with both countries.

That is a difficult balancing act. On Thursday, when Israel's President Isaac Herzog addressed a regional security summit hosted by Azerbaijan in Baku, delegations from Turkey, Iran and other countries walked out of the hall.

articles.title: Letters with 'suspicious substances' sent to US election offices
articles.summary: A number of states have confirmed they were targeted by the mailings, including Oklahoma, Ohio and Louisiana.
body: Federal authorities say they are investigating "potentially hazardous" letters containing "suspicious substances" that have been sent to congressional and state election offices around the US.
The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) said they were trying to trace the "suspicious mailings", some of which were intercepted before they were received.
Authorities declined to say how many offices had been targeted, but several secretaries of state and congressional offices reported receiving the letters.
Coming just weeks before the US midterm elections, it echoes previous security scares involving suspicious mail.
"This FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens," the agencies said in a statement on Thursday.
The Oklahoma State Election Board and the Louisiana secretary of state both said this week that their offices had received letters containing a white powder.
The Louisiana office was evacuated after a staff member opened the package on Tuesday, but it has since reopened after law enforcement found no evidence of harmful substances.
Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was the intended recipient of a letter containing white powder, but the USPIS had intercepted it.
Senator Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, was also sent a letter containing a suspicious substance, but it was intercepted before reaching the office, his spokesman said.
The New York State Capitol in Albany and the Wyoming State Capitol in Cheyenne also received suspicious packages, according to emergency responder scanner feed reviewed by the BBC.
The suspicious mailings come just weeks before election day, which will determine the balance of power in Congress.
Ahead of the 2024 election, vote officials in 17 states received suspicious packages.
A year earlier, suspicious envelopes, some laced with fentanyl, were sent to election offices in at least five states.

articles.title: Two dead in Istanbul after heaviest rainfall in 84 years, governor says
articles.summary: Residents have been told to avoid leaving their homes unless absolutely necessary.
body: Flooding in the Kucukcekmece district of Istanbul
Two people have died after severe flooding caused by what the governor of Istanbul said was the heaviest rainfall in 84 years, BBC Turkish has reported.
A14-year-old boy died after he was electrocuted when he stepped in a puddle, while a 34-year-old man attempting to cross the road slipped and fell, hitting his head on the pavement.
Nearly 600 people have been rescued after becoming stranded, the city's deputy mayor said, with cars submerged in water in some districts.
Residents have been told by Istanbul Governor Davut Gül to avoid leaving their homes unless absolutely necessary.
The city's governorship is investigating the death of the teenaged boy who was electrocuted.

Some areas of Istanbul have seen rainfall equivalent to one seventh of the annual average, according to the interior minister. Schools were ordered to close on Thursday and Friday, as the rain is expected to continue.
Nuri Aslan, deputy mayor of the city, said 595 people had been evacuated to safe areas after becoming trapped, while more than 8,000 workers were responding to the flooding.
"I urge all our citizens to remain vigilant against the expected heavy rain and storm, particularly during nighttime hours," he wrote on X.
He told people to use public transport instead of private vehicles, with the city's metro hours expanded to 02:00 local time.
The flooding also impacted air travel, with 46 planes unable to land at airports in Istanbul, BBC Turkish said.

A car park in a shopping centre was flooded in the Sariyer district, with multiple vehicles submerged. Sections of roads in other areas collapsed, according to local media, and a river has burst its banks.
More than 16 million people live in the broader Istanbul metropolitan area. The interior ministry has also warned of sudden flooding in several provinces.

In response, employees who are disabled, pregnant or veterans will be granted administrative leave on Thursday, unless they work in health, safety, and rainwater drainage fields, Turkish media reported. Women working in the public sector who have children under the age of eight will also be granted leave.

articles.title: Obama says drift towards extremism 'not inevitable'
articles.summary: More than 12,000 people filled a major venue in the city to hear the former US president's take on the challenges the world is facing. .
body: Barack Obama warned that online platforms were stoking anger and fear in people
Barack Obama has told an audience in Glasgow that hope is worth fighting for despite big challenges facing the modern world.
The 44th president of the United States said online platforms had shifted in recent years to focus on content that stoked anger and fear, but he believes a drift to extremism is "not inevitable".
The comments came as he addressed an OVO Hydro crowd of 12,150 people while in conversation with British journalist and author Sathnam Sanghera, part of three speaking dates in the UK.
He reflected on his time in the White House and examined the political and social challenges facing the US and the wider world.
More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland
Obama said that during his presidential campaign in 2008, when social media and technology was gaining traction, he had seen them as a beacon for hope
But he said the same positive forces and tools that could mobilise people around democracy or human rights could also be used by hate groups.
He said they "connected people for good, but also for ill".
"It turns out that the reptilian side of our brain really gets attracted to anger, fear, resentment and the sense that someone is out to get you," he said.
"So a lot of social media and a lot of our information is informed around that."
But the former president, who has already spoken in Belfast and will appear in Manchester on Thursday night, said that a drift towards extremism was "not inevitable".

He added: "After World War Two, at least in the United States and certainly in Europe as well, the federal government said 'we're going to set up some rules because we've seen what propaganda can do in the hands of somebody like Hitler.
"We can see how big lies and misinformation can distort and enrage and incite violence. So we're going to hold these folks responsible'."
"We have not chosen to do that."
The former President was speaking at the OVO Hydro
Obama, who was president until 2016, said there was a "critical balance" that must be struck between free speech and regulation.
But the 65-year-old said that the world and its leaders are going to need to find mechanisms and new institutions to allow rigorous debate and disagreement while helping people sort out basic facts.
He said: "If I had a blame pie for why politics is so polarised and why we're seeing a rise of populism in many places, it's because of that information that is going into our brains every day."
Obama said this resulted in young people feeling discouraged, and that "it's not a healthy diet that our brains are on at the moment".
He added that he feared this could become even worse with AI making it hard to distinguish between what is true and what is not, something he believes will make democracy hard to function.

Speaking about hope, Obama was asked if he still believed in a Martin Luther King Jr phrase he quoted years ago, about the arm of the moral universe being long, but ultimately bending towards justice.
The former president said that he still stands by the quote and argued that hope is an active "almost theological" choice people must make.
He said: "It is a decision about how do we face and embrace this finite amount of time we have on the planet."
He told the audience he believes it is healthier for people to believe that change is possible.
"I think when we act on that basis, it doesn't always work out, but over time things do get better," he said.
Obama also said there seems to be a cycle in humanity where people forget lessons learned from the past and start to take things for granted.
"We start thinking 'maybe using language in public from our politicians that fosters hatred and scapegoats certain people – immigrants, Jews, or blacks or gays – that's just talk, it's humour'."
He said people forget where that can lead to, with them becoming less tolerant.
Obama told the audience that the world is going to be dealing with "big challenges", but he said he thinks "we can be better" and that making the world better remains worth fighting for.

articles.title: Brazil's Congress approves shorter working week in win for Lula
articles.summary: Lula's supporters hope the measure will boost his popularity ahead of a presidential run-off in 10 days.
body: The measure had broad support and trade unions held rallies in its favour in recent weeks
Brazil's Congress has approved a constitutional amendment that will cut the working week from 44 hours to 40 and give employees two days off per week without cutting their salary.
The change represents the biggest overhaul to workers' rights since Brazil's return to democracy in 1988.
Senators passed the amendment, which left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had championed, less than two weeks before a second round in the Latin American nation's presidential election.

Lula's supporters are hoping that its passage, which is estimated to benefit more than 30 million workers, will boost his chances of closing in on his right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the 25 October run-off.

The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro won the first round of the presidential election with 47% of the vote, ahead of Lula on 45.2%. Both fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round.
Opinion polls suggest that the move to cut the working week is very popular, with one nationwide survey finding that almost 70% of Brazilians backed it.
The measure had already passed in the Chamber of Deputies, Brazil's lower house, in May, before senators overwhelmingly backed the measure on Wednesday by 75 votes to one.
Flávio Bolsonaro, who is currently a senator, dropped his previous opposition to the measure and also cast a "yes" vote.

Announcing his change of heart on Tuesday, he argued that he had been swayed by the measure's popularity, commenting: "Most Brazilian workers ‌want to ⁠see the end of the six-day workweek, so I'm going to vote in favour of ending it."
The younger Bolsonaro had earlier denounced the proposal as an "opportunistic" attempt by his presidential rival to appeal to working-class voters.
Before his about-turn, he had said that it should be down to employees and employers to agree on a work schedule, rather than restrictions being imposed by a constitutional amendment.
Lula described Bolsonaro's policy reversal as "electoral opportunism" and celebrated the amendment's approval, saying it would make a real difference to workers.
"It means more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow up, look after yourself and enjoy life," he wrote on social media.
Parent groups were among those to back the change
Critics of the measure have warned that it will raise production costs, which will eventually be passed on to the consumer, resulting in higher prices.
But its supporters argue that having two days off a week will allow workers to be better rested and therefore more productive in the hours that they do work.
The change is due to be phased in, with the working week first being shortened to 42 hours after a two-month grace period and then again to 40 hours at a later stage.
The changes will take more than a year to entirely take effect but many of its backers are already celebrating.
Luciana de Almeida, 36, who works six days a week as a cashier in a supermarket, said it would "make a lot of difference" to her life.
The single mother, who lives in Rio de Janeiro, said she has been missing out on time with her three children as the only day off she had was usually spent doing domestic chores.
"My body, and my mind in particular, are very tired," she told BBC Brasil.
"I need time with my daughters, have some leisure time, or even just some time resting at home."

articles.title: Brooklyn novelty shop reeling from 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
articles.summary: Art of Play says its staff have been threatened after the singer complained online about how she was treated.
body: Watch: What's going on between Kelly Clarkson and a Brooklyn store bird?
On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.
Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby in this Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"

Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.
The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000).

"Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a shop, who imply she cannot afford various items.
In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable".
Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale.
It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000.
They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day.
"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said.
"It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."
Molly the mechanical bird now has a price tag of $15m
Clarkson defended her decision to criticise the store on social media, saying: "I never blast people but you my friend were an exception."
When the BBC visited the store on Wednesday, there were more reporters than customers.
A shopkeeper said they would not comment on the story anymore and just wanted to get back to business as usual.
Molly still hung on the wall at the shop, this time next to a price tag of $15m.
The sign jokes that the sculpture is the "world's most famous singing bird automata!"
The store's owner has said he and his staff have faced threats and harassment after Clarkson's complaint, telling the BBC's US partner CBS News that the singer had endangered them.
This week, a man filmed himself yelling expletives outside the store, before accusing its employees of "racially profiling" Clarkson.
Customer Emily Trantanella likes Art of Play
The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit.
The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird.
She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier.
But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises.
One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy.
For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise.
Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days.
Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here.

articles.title: Actor Imran Khan ordered to leave India after participating in protest
articles.summary: The Bollywood actor had been detained and released while participating in a protest in Mumbai on 10 October.
body: Imran Khan had been briefly detained by the police on 10 October while participating in a protest in Mumbai
Authorities in India have ordered actor Imran Khan, nephew of Bollywood star Aamir Khan, to leave the country by 28 October after he participated in a protest, seeking electoral reforms.
An American citizen, Khan holds an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card, which allows people of Indian origin to visit and stay in the country. But an OCI cannot vote or contest elections.
"Imran Khan participated in the agitation at Mumbai's August Kranti Maidan, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar," police said in a statement on Thursday.
Khan's lawyer has said the actor will challenge the order in the Bombay High Court.
Police said the Foreigners' Regional Registration Office (FRRO) had served Khan a notice for violating laws by protesting.
But the actor's lawyer said that no provision of the law or any rule for OCI cardholders prohibit him from participating in a protest.
The Press Trust of India reports that the actor's petition against the Mumbai police notice termed it as "drastic".
Khan is known for the 2008 hit romantic comedy Jaane Tu... Ya Jaane Na.
He first appeared as a child actor in popular films such as Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak in 1988 and Jo Jeeta Wohi Sikandar in 1992.
Since his debut as a lead actor in 2008, he has starred in a number of films like I Hate Luv Storys, Mere Brother Ki Dulhan and Delhi Belly.
The notice to leave the country comes as Khan returns to acting this year with the Netflix film Adhure Hum Adhure Tum after a hiatus of over a decade.
Khan also shared a photo from inside the detention van on his Instagram page

On 10 October, the actor participated in the protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a wider GenZ-led movement that has been holding demonstrations for days seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of India's top election official over allegations of vote fraud. India's poll panel denies these charges.
"Imran Khan had participated in the agitation despite not being an Indian citizen," police said in their statement.

The complaint against Khan was lodged by Kirit Somaiya, a leader of India's and the state's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), who accused the actor of being "involved in a conspiracy to spread anarchy in India".
Khan did not address Somaiya's allegation directly, but had spoken to reporters about his participation in the protest.
"I don't have demands. I'm here as a citizen, as a person who lives in this city. I'm here to see why freedom of movement is being restricted, why people's voices are being suppressed," he'd said.
He added that he was not at the protest as the representative of any organisation.
Following the protest, Khan was briefly detained by the police along with other protesters.

He posted a photo of himself inside the police detention van on Instagram with the caption, "Apparently I'm going for a drive." The post received more than two million likes on the social media platform.

Over the weekend, thousands of protesters had marched in Delhi, Mumbai and other parts of India, demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar ahead of crucial state elections in response to the CJP's call.
On Monday, leaders of many of India's main opposition parties, including Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, led thousands of protesters in a march from Connaught Place to the Supreme Court in Delhi.
On Wednesday, two top CJP leaders were sent to jail for five days after being arrested for allegedly trespassing at a protest site in Delhi.
The CJP has called for another protest on Friday evening in the capital.

articles.title: Australian woman charged with lacing colleague's curry with snail poison
articles.summary: The alleged victim, who was in a relationship with the woman, had spotted bright green pellets in the meal.
body: An Australian woman has been charged after allegedly lacing a colleague's curry with snail poison.
Police in the state of Western Australia say the alleged victim made a meal for her co-workers in February, which they shared at morning tea.
But when the 58-year-old returned to eat leftovers at lunch, she noticed bright green granules in the food and that her tongue felt numb after tasting it.

The accused - who was in a relationship with the alleged victim - has been charged with endangering the life, health or safety of another person after a months-long investigation, and will face court on 5 November.
Police allege the 43-year-old woman - who hasn't been named - visited a chemical storage shed before returning to the staffroom where the curry was kept.
After tasting it, the alleged victim handed the meal over to detectives, who identified the substance as snail pellets containing metaldehyde, a poisonous substance.
Commissioner Col Blanch told reporters the poison can cause serious injury or death.
"We're just very thankful that the person who tasted the curry was aware of something that wasn't quite right," he said, according to the Seven Network.

articles.title: North Korea and China open new bridge after 12-year delay
articles.summary: China is the North's largest trading partner and a lifeline against the sanctions Pyongyang faces.
body: The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea
A long-delayed road bridge linking China and North Korea has opened, Chinese state media report, as trade ties improve between the neighbours.
China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a lifeline against heavy international sanctions over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme.
The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea, and is set to become the main land route for trade between them.
Its launch, initially slated for 2014, had been indefinitely postponed after North Korea halted construction of its roads and customs facilities, as relations with Beijing turned frosty.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang, in a video address on Thursday, said the bridge was a "new landmark symbolising the traditional friendship between China and North Korea", and that the two countries were "opening a new chapter" in bilateral ties.
The New Yalu River Bridge is an alternative to the decades-old Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which was built between 1937 and 1943 during Imperial Japan's occupation of the region.

The new bridge is an "important facility for connectivity" between the two countries, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday, adding that the route would "further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges".
Last year, bilateral trade reached $2.7bn, marking a recovery to pre-pandemic levels, mostly fuelled by Chinese exports to North Korea.

A sharp and sudden increase in trade across the border is "unlikely" as the UN sanctions on North Korea remain in effect, Kang Jun-young, a professor of Chinese studies at the Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, tells the BBC.
"Pyongyang is also wary of a sudden flood of Chinese imports that would greatly expand China's influence over its domestic market," he adds.
"China is well aware of these concerns, so trade is more likely to grow gradually."

Beijing and Pyongyang are long-standing allies with a mutual defence treaty, the only one that China has with any country. The relationship is often described "as close as lips and teeth", a remark first made by China's former leader Mao Zedong.
Watch: Why did Xi Jinping visit North Korea?
But the alliance is not without tension.

Ties were frosty for much of the 2010s as Beijing's patience over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme wore thin. Kim Jong Un conducted a nuclear test in 2017 and has since ramped up tests of banned ballistic missiles - all of which increased US wariness, and strengthened its military alliances with South Korea and Japan.
China's attitude has shifted more recently.

"Whilst only a decade ago, Beijing was overtly critical of North Korea's nuclearisation - and indeed calling for Pyongyang's denuclearisation - China is now saying little, if anything, to this effect," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford, tells the BBC.
Observers say one reason is that North Korea has grown closer to Russia because of the Ukraine war.

At least 2,300 North Korean soldiers are believed to have died fighting for Russia in Ukraine. In return, Russia supplies North Korea with oil, in violation of UN sanctions. In 2024, Russia was estimated to have sent more than a billion barrels of oil as payment for Pyongyang's weapons and troops.
Last month, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge, which Russian state media said would allow the movement of up to 300 vehicles and more than 2,000 people every day.
So Beijing is believed to be trying to reassert its sway over Pyongyang by rekindling ties.
Air China resumed direct flights between Beijing and Pyongyang in March after a six-year hiatus triggered by the pandemic. The two countries reopened passenger train services the same month.
Chinese President Xi Jinping's first state visit of this year, in June, was to Pyongyang, where he met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

"The opening of the New Yalu River Bridge demonstrates bilateral relations are improving and that Xi Jinping's June visit to North Korea was more than symbolic," says Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.
"But the long delay, including North Korea's pandemic self-isolation and domestic socioeconomic crackdowns, shows what a difficult partner Pyongyang can be for Beijing."

articles.title: Indian woman and boyfriend get death sentence in 'blue drum' murder case
articles.summary: The body was recovered from a large blue plastic storage container - locally called a drum.
body: Sahil Shukla and Muskan Rastogi were found guilty of the murder on 30 September
Warning: This story contains details that some readers may find distressing.
A woman and her boyfriend have been sentenced to death for the murder of her husband in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh.
Muskan Rastogi, 26, and Sahil Shukla, 28, were convicted on 30 September by a court in Meerut city for the 2025 murder of her husband Saurabh Rajput.
Rajput's body was recovered from a large blue plastic storage container - locally called a drum - leading to the case being dubbed as "the blue drum murder".
Wednesday's death sentences have to be confirmed by the high court. Rastogi and Shukla have the option to challenge the verdict.
The prosecution said in court that Rastogi and Shukla had been classmates in school and had grown close in the absence of Rajput who worked in London.
When Rajput first came to know of their affair in 2021, he had wanted to get a divorce but was persuaded against this by his family since the couple had a young daughter.
Rajput was murdered on 3 March 2025 when he was visiting Meerut. Police said he was given food laced with sedatives by Rastogi before he was killed.
Rastogi and Shukla fled to Himachal Pradesh state but used Rajput's mobile phone to send text messages to his family to make it seem like he was alive and travelling for business, they added.
A few days later, however, Rajput's family lodged a complaint with the police saying that he was missing.
On 17 March, when Rastogi visited her parents after returning from Himachal Pradesh, her six-year-old daughter asked about her father.
Rastogi initially blamed her in-laws for her husband's murder. Unconvinced, her parental family took her to the police station.
Rastogi confessed to the crime during interrogation and she and Shukla were arrested and charged with the murder.
"My brother was killed by cruel people," Rajput's brother told BBC Hindi.
Rastogi's parents also demanded strict action against her.
"My daughter, along with a friend, murdered her husband in her own home. She is not fit for this society and is a danger to others," her father told ANI news agency.
Rastogi gave birth to a second child while in jail.

articles.title: Student protesters attack government buildings in Tirana
articles.summary: Thousands of students in Albania are calling for better university conditions and job prospects, but buildings have been set on fire in the unrest.
body: The scene in Tirana, Albania's capital on Wednesday
Thousands of students have taken to the streets in the Albanian capital of Tirana, attacking several government buildings on the second day of violent anti-government protests.
The demonstration began outside the ministry of education on Tuesday, as students called for better university conditions and job prospects.
Wednesday saw part of the education ministry's building set on fire, while the prime minister's office, finance and interior ministry, and several surrounding businesses were also attacked.
Albania's Deputy Prime Minister ​Albana Koçiu has called for "calmness, self-restraint and maturity" and said "Albania does not need to burn to change".
Dozens of protesters wearing gas masks and balaclavas were seen throwing rocks and firecrackers through the education ministry's gates
Riot police have clashed with the protesters, using tear gas and water cannons to disperse them.
One demonstrator, Enida Bimi, told Reuters news agency that the protest is not just for the students, but "for all the people of Albania".

"The people are very angry at the system. They need to change everything. With this corruption all around, the crime and everything else is happening. And the people now are angry. They need to change the system," Bimi said.
Another protester, Arber Leshi, said people are angry at "the most corrupt government our country has ever seen".
Education Mirela Kumbaro said that while she respects the right to protest, "civic student protest and violence against public buildings and property are two different things".
Protester Enida Bimi said people "are very angry at the system"
Officials have criticised the behaviour of some protesters.

"Setting fire to an institution is not a peaceful protest. It is an act that endanger's peoples lives", said economy minister Delina Ibrahimaj, responding to a video appearing to show protesters throwing rocks at the finance ministry building.
Sixteen people were arrested "in connection with violent acts" during Tuesday's protest, Albania's state-run news agency said.
Sali Berisha, the leader of the opposition - the Democratic Party of Albania - has praised the protesters.
"The streets and squares of Tirana have never seen lions like these students," he said during an evening meeting on Wednesday, Albania's state-run news agency Ata reported.
This student-led protest comes after months of anti-government protests, known as the Flamingo Revolution, which is calling for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
The protests were sparked by a luxury tourism project linked to Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, which fuelled anger over alleged corruption and a lack of transparency from Rama's government.

articles.title: Fiery speeches, LED hats and infighting: inside an Alberta separatist conference
articles.summary: WeUnify’s Reclaiming Alberta brought together ardent supporters of independence from Canada while highlighting key disagreements over strategy – not least how close a free Alberta should be to the US
body: The debate began with a simple question in a dark Calgary hotel ballroom: does Alberta need Canada?

By the time the audience was asked to vote at the end, more than three-quarters had answered no – a decisive measure of the convictions of a room packed with some of Alberta’s most ardent independence supporters, some of whom had paid C$900 (£480) for a “visionary” weekend pass.

But outside the comfort of the ballroom, the debate is far from settled. Across the province, the forthcoming 19 October referendum on separatism has divided communities, prompting accusations of treason and grift and, at times, bitter feuds between former allies. One recent poll shows support for independence at only 14%.
You wouldn’t know it from the WeUnify’s Reclaiming Alberta conference though.

“This is a matter of survival,” conservative activist and broadcaster Faytene Grasseschi told the crowd, which erupted into applause after she said Alberta’s oil resources had been “usurped” by the federal government and the Canada she had been born into “doesn’t exist any more”.

In the main halls outside the ballroom, attendees milled around the vendor stalls. A handful donned a $6,500 (£4,925) helmet that resembles white colanders hastily attached to a bike helmet, bathing the user’s head in red LED light supposedly for treatment of “Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s, dementia, traumatic brain injury, [and] brain fog”. Others took in sales pitches about the need for gold and silver as paper money “fails”.

But the busiest stall belonged to the group Let’s Talk Alberta. It says it is neither a political party nor a campaign organisation but its five bound pamphlets include a 52-page volume titled Every Argument to Stay is a Reason to Leave. The pamphlets were written by its founder, Chris Scott, a cafe owner who attracted widespread attention during the Covid-19 pandemic after he was arrested for violating public health orders. After a lengthy legal battle, he was acquitted.

On stage, Scott told the crowd the push for independence would be a “wake-up call” for the rest of the country and reflected a fight against what many in the movement see as an entrenched political elite – a fight that needed to happen “come hell or high water”.

After initial efforts to bring a referendum question on independence were derailed by First Nations groups, Albertans will now be voting on the question of whether Alberta should remain part of Canada or whether the provincial government should begin the legal process to hold a second, binding referendum on separation. With just days to go, the foot soldiers and the faithful of the independence movement have begun their final pitches for what they envision will one day be a wealthy, “anti-woke” nation – one unshackled from the control of the federal government, or even a vassal of the United States.
Related: ‘Truly terrifying’: Alberta voter data breach raises fears for Canada’s electoral integrity

The conference, which was organised by the WeUnify movement, brought together Alberta separatists, veterans of the pandemic-era “freedom movement” and conservatives united by a distrust of established institutions.

Speakers reserved their harshest words for Justin Trudeau, who, despite resigning as prime minister more than a year ago, remains a bugbear for the separatist movement. Sheane Meikle, a volunteer with Let’s Talk Alberta, said the independence movement was gaining support.
“We’re getting far fewer Trudeau salutes when we wave flags on the side of the road,” he said – a reference to the raised middle finger.

Meikle, 58, has spent months travelling the province with Scott, adding more than 32,000 miles to his van as part of a quest to convince sceptical Albertans of the benefits of separation. The referendum had been “longtime coming” for the movement, he said. “Even if the results don’t go our way, it doesn’t mean we’re done. This is a movement now that’s sustained.”

Not everyone agreed the conference was the best idea, though. Keith Wilson, one of the principal intellectual and legal architects of Alberta’s modern separatist movement, admitted in an interview that he regretted participating. “It’s just an echo chamber in there – I’m not changing any minds that are already made up for separatism. I shouldn’t be here. I should be out campaigning.”
In September Wilson brought together 45 unnamed contributors to publish the Alberta Transition Plan, a 214-page blueprint for turning Alberta from a province into an independent country.

“We have everything. Alberta is an economic powerhouse. But we’re also on the ground with our face in our dirt and our arms tied behind our backs because of Ottawa,” he said, referring to a longstanding belief that the federal government continues to exert unfair influence over the oil-rich province. “That’s how many Albertans feel, and that’s why they want change.”

His blueprint, however, has drawn criticism for leaving major questions about the costs and practicalities of independence unresolved. The University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy recently estimated that the costs associated with separation could cost Alberta between C$50bn and C$170bn over its first five years and warned substantial annual deficits were possible.

Nor have the secessionists built the political machinery that could bring it about. The campaign has no official leader, nor an organised movement under the guise of a political party. No elected officials have campaigned for independence. Unlike Quebec, where independence parties have run explicitly on the idea and won, Alberta has only ever elected a separatist candidate once, and he lost his seat months later. In previous elections, separatist parties have won an average popular vote of 1%.

In the absence of coherent leadership, prominent figures have been thrust into the limelight, often with chaotic results. Jeff Rath, a bombastic lawyer linked to the Alberta Prosperity Project, is embroiled in legal battles over allegations that millions of dollars in disputed First Nations trust funds were mishandled. Mitch Sylvestre, head of the Alberta Prosperity Project and owner of a sporting goods store, told the Toronto Star he fears King Charles will have him assassinated. David Parker, a longtime rightwing political organizer, was at the centre of a voter-data scandal that exposed the personal information of nearly 3 million Albertans and remains under investigation.

But for Meikle and others, the movement is “grassroots” and would only be damaged by the presence of elected officials. “We just need our politicians to get out of the way and stop being so biased towards this movement,” he said. “They shouldn’t be using taxpayer money to campaign against us.”

For many here, the coronavirus pandemic remains an animating force. Some of the panellists and speakers were prominent lawyers who challenged and in some cases won cases against the government for overreach in shutdown laws.

It was the pandemic – and the political atmosphere that followed it – that got Betty Field, a retiree who worked in the oil sector, interested in the independence movement. Her husband, Gord Pick, chimed in that even supporters of federalism should vote against unity “to put a little fear of God into Ottawa”.

But the lack of a leader has led to divergence over messaging and strategy. In early October, the Globe and Mail reported on ties between the Alberta separatists movement and Republican operatives, and meetings between those unelected Albertans and White House staff. Among items allegedly discussed were oil revenues that could be directed to the US in exchange for assistance establishing a new country, as well as Alberta’s fresh water resources.
“We wouldn’t want to be part of the US,” said Pick. “Why trade one overlord in Ottawa for another in Washington?”

Outside, fresh off their weekly dinner of liver and onions – “just the best in Calgary, hands down!” – friends Vera Patten and Lisette Bourget stand in the waning sun, smoking a cigarette. When a conference attender offers to hold the door for them, Patten says politely: “Oh we’re not with you.”

“I hope they lose,” she adds after a small crowd, also out for a smoke, returns back inside. “It’s just disgusting. I can’t believe how they’re trying to break up this country.” A veteran of the oil industry, Patten has lived in Calgary for decades and says only damage can come from separation. “This needs to stop, and I’m hopeful that after the vote – that they lose.”
Wilson said the movement had other plans.

“The separatist movement in Alberta started before my parents were born – and they’re dead,” he said. “Because if you’re a separatist, you see a better opportunity for your friends, neighbours and your grandkids. And you never give up on that. Even if the vote goes poorly, it will not end. In the same way that winters won’t end and springs won’t end, this movement won’t end either. It’s here to stay.”

articles.title: ‘Clean air is not a favour’: Indonesia’s neighbours fed up with acrid haze as Singapore threatens to prosecute
articles.summary: Millions affected by smoke from wildfires as schools close, respiratory illnesses soar and diplomatic tensions rise
body: Singapore is threatening to prosecute companies responsible for some of the worst fires in years in neighbouring Indonesia, as the region grows increasingly frustrated with a persistent, acrid haze that could result in diplomatic relations fraying.

Lawrence Wong, the Singaporean prime minister, said his government was distributing masks to vulnerable citizens and working with countries in the region to deal with the smoke. “At the same time, we are looking into which companies may be responsible for the fires,” he said in a Facebook post on Thursday, adding that he was exploring the idea of “joint action with other countries”.
Related: ‘The physical toll is visceral’: How Indonesia’s fire haze affects millions - visual guide
Singapore has no plantations or forests of its own, but several companies with concessions in Indonesia are reportedly based in the city-state.

Haze is a persistent problem in Indonesia, but drier-than-usual conditions mean the thick smoke has been drifting into nearby Singapore, Malaysia, Brunei and Timor-Leste, and as far afield as the Philippines and Vietnam. Millions are affected, with school closures, respiratory illness spiking and air pollution indexes reaching unhealthy levels.
Malaysians and Singaporeans have been sharing images online of their cities, with skyscrapers disappearing into the smog, and frustration with the region’s most populous country is boiling over.

“Year after year, the haze comes back. It affects our health, closes schools, hurts businesses, and costs us billions,” a veteran Malaysian social activist and former politician wrote in a public letter this week. Lee Lam Thye said that real enforcement and “not just polite words” were needed. “Those responsible must be named, investigated, and punished. Clean air is not a favour. It is a basic right.”

While Indonesia regularly battles wildfires in the dry season, these blazes are the most intense in more than a decade and exacerbated by slash-and-burn practices to clear land for agriculture, including palm oil, of which Indonesia is the world’s largest producer.

Regional diplomats have offered to help Indonesia, but their offers have not always been immediately accepted. On Monday, an Indonesian official said the country was “still capable of handling it”. By the end of the week, Jakarta said it would accept assistance

Such delicate diplomacy is routine among the region’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), which is built on ​quiet engagement and non-interference. A meeting of regional foreign ministers in the Philippines is due next month, but that might be too late.

Nerves are fraying. In remarks that went viral on social media, Syahganda Nainggolan, the head of Indonesia’s government communication agency, hit back at the criticism on Saturday. “We don’t only send haze,” he said, “the oxygen in Singapore and Malaysia comes from our forests.”

Rare strong words came earlier this month from Anwar Ibrahim, the Malaysian prime minister. He said he had been in contact with Indonesia’s president, Prabowo Subianto, “who agreed to take the necessary steps, and this commitment must be followed by immediate and effective action from the Indonesian side to tackle the root causes of the haze”.
At the same time, pressure is growing on Jakarta to declare a national disaster, first from civil society groups but now also from Indonesian politicians and neighbours.

According to the Jakarta Post, Indonesian students have been holding protests across Kalimantan and Sumatra, demanding accountability and government action. In one video posted online, a child in a mask stands outside under a dark orange sky and calls on the local and national government to help. He holds a sign that says: “Save our little lungs”.
The country has dispatched firefighters and announced a crackdown on arsonists, but declaring a disaster would unlock funds and help thousands with medical expenses.
On Friday, the Indonesian forestry ministry said four firefighters were killed in a national park in Java.

Longtime onlookers say the issue is not just firefighting, but targeting the companies involved. In recent years, several attempts to take legal action against the companies exacerbating “transboundary haze” have failed, both locally and internationally, and posed a diplomatic minefield.

Haze is complex for Singapore and Malaysia, as they host companies working in Indonesia. A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia that it claimed were linked to burning land in Indonesia.

Ultimately, Indonesians bear the brunt of the blazes. The health ministry has reported nearly 280,000 people in the country with respiratory infections linked to the fires, with children under five accounting for more than 60,000.

Michelle Dyonisius, a campaigner at Amnesty International Indonesia, said rights groups and civil society organisations were ramping up pressure on the government to declare a national disaster emergency. “It has been going on for months, affecting millions and millions of people, including abroad,” she said.

“I think there is a refusal to acknowledge the gravity of the issue at hand and also the belief that it is under control. But considering the gravity of the issue and all of the people affected, it seems quite naive to remain in that position.”

articles.title: Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries ‘a disgrace’
articles.summary: US president says Zelenskyy ‘more difficult ​to deal with ​than Putin’ after ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses
body: Donald Trump has called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy after an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.

Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries ⁠after Zelenskyy said Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire unilaterally declared by Trump on Sunday, having briefly halted its attacks to demonstrate its readiness for peace talks. Russia had continued its strikes on Ukrainian power plants.
Related: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses
In an interview with Newsmax aired on Thursday, the US president said: “All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that’s a disgrace.

“There are a lot ‌of targets you can ‌hit, but when you shoot at diesel refineries where you make, you know, ‌diesel oil, and we need that, and the world needs that, then he’s not doing a good service for the world.”
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since Trump announced an easing sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel on to global markets.

Zelenskyy criticised the agreement, which was widely interpreted as an attempt to curb high fuel prices before the US midterm elections, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than four and a half years ago. US efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.

Trump repeated to Newsmax his views of the two leaders involved in the conflict. “I’m not a big fan of Zelenskyy,” Trump said. “I think they actually both would like to see it ⁠end, but I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult ​to deal with ​than Putin.”

Arriving in Brussels to meet EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy did not comment on Trump’s latest remarks. He said he was “so thankful that we have such huge support from the EU” and its leaders, whom he described as “real leaders”.
He went on to say that Ukraine wanted to end the war as quickly as possible, but “we don’t see now signals from [the] Russian side that they are ready for this”.

Kyiv’s relationship with Washington was strained further this week when Ukraine said Starlink services had been restricted, in effect hobbling Ukrainian drone strike missions and crucial air defences with a flick of the switch.
During a visit to London this week, the Ukrainian president said the sudden restriction of Starlink had left him feeling personally betrayed by Trump and lamented losing a partner.
Related: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses

The British defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said on Thursday that his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, had assured him in a face-to-face meeting that the vital satellite communications system had been restored. In an interview with the BBC, he said it was unclear what had caused the disruption, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.”
Amid growing doubts about long-term US commitment to Ukraine, European leaders declared their support for Zelenskyy.

Standing alongside the Ukrainian leader in Brussels, the European Council president, António Costa, said Ukraine could “count on us not only to support you in war” but also in the path to negotiating EU membership.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU had supported Trump’s energy ceasefire, “but we have seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute” and instead had escalated its attacks. She said the EU intended to increase pressure on Russia, promising a 22nd round of sanctions, adding: “We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war.”
The promise of further European sanctions against Russia comes weeks after the EU lifted sanctions against two prominent Russian oligarchs at the request of France and Luxembourg.
After meeting Zelenskyy, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said it was “crucial” that Ukraine received “all the means necessary to protect itself”.
The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, posted online: “I can reassure you, dear Ukrainian friends and President Zelenskyy: YOU ARE NOT ALONE.”
As Zelenskyy met Macron in Brussels, he said that the Kremlin had “launched yet another vile drone strike on Ukrainian energy infrastructure” in the city of Lutsk, which caused blackouts.
The Kremlin, meanwhile, accused Ukraine of derailing US peace efforts by resuming its strikes on refineries.

articles.title: Friday briefing: How Manchester City’s ​financial scandal could upend the whole football league
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: Manchester City’s disgrace reaches far beyond sport, exposing not just a crisis in football but also raising questions about foreign owned British institutions
body: Good morning. It’s a sporting scandal of colossal proportions, with the juiciest details still to come. Manchester City’s ascent from mediocre to majestic changed the landscape of British football. Now, that pace looks set to be matched by a sudden, plummeting fall.

The club has been found guilty of breaching football finance rules to the tune of hundreds of millions of pounds, with ramifications poised to spill far beyond Manchester (the club denies the allegations, and says it will appeal). Foreign state ownership makes this an international relations issue, not just a sporting one. The prime minister has been dragged into the sleaze-fest, and the stream of stories shows no sign of slowing. Meanwhile, the Mancunian club has the chutzpah to sit at the top of the Premier League, much to the repulsion of my Manchester United-supporting boyfriend.

With the help of Guardian football writer Jonathan Wilson, today’s First Edition delivers everything you need to know about the crisis engulfing the beautiful game, and believe me, this one’s not just for the footie fans. That’s after the headlines.

Ukraine | Wes Streeting urged the US to stand by Ukraine on his visit to the American capital and sought to cool tensions between the two countries in the wake of the Starlink row that is threatening to set back Kyiv’s war effort.

UK news | Jeffrey Donaldson has been sentenced to 15 years for sexual offences against two women who were children when he abused them, completing what was described as a “catastrophic descent into disgrace”.
Hacking | An Israeli advertising agency has been serving millions of online adverts that allow “zero-click” spyware to be used against targets, researchers at a Canadian university have said.
UK news | A woman has alleged Russell Brand told her “it’s just fun” as he raped her in a hotel room at the 1999 Labour party conference, a court has heard.
US news | Donald Trump has shelved a widely condemned plan to livestream the execution of a disabled man by firing squad.

To some (Manchester City fans, mostly), it was a sporting success story for the ages. After decades of underachievement, a middle-of-the-road club transformed into England’s best performing – and top title-winning – team. Others grumbled that City’s success was a sad indictment of the state of modern football. The club’s change in fortunes came shortly after they were bought by the Abu Dhabi United Group, a private equity group owned by the Gulf state’s vice president. Billionaires had already gutted the topflight of its heart, now governments with entire GDPs to burn had descended.

Except, of course, the cash injection at Manchester City breached strict Premier League limits. Financial fair play rules, introduced by the league in 2013, aimed to keep a lid on spending so that clubs – financed by, say, a fossil-fuel rich state – couldn’t simply spend billions for immediate dominance. Only, that’s precisely what Manchester City did. According to an independent panel, they secretly boosted their income by a staggering £900m between 2009 and 2018.

When he first flicked through the panel’s 40-page verdict summary, Wilson was surprised by the “incredibly strong language it used for a dry legal document”. The word “sham” is repeated eight times. “There was a clear sense that the panel felt systematically lied to by City,” says Wilson.
The real spice is likely to come in the yet-to-be-published appendices to the verdict, which will probably contain names, companies and detailed figures.

These recent revelations didn’t come out of nowhere. Back in November 2018, German newspaper Der Spiegel published a four-part series on Manchester City (“Bending the Rules to the Tune of Millions” was the first headline). The paper’s bombshell reporting was based on data released in The Football Leaks, a website containing millions of documents on allegedly murky financial transactions in the sport, made public by Portuguese whistleblower (and convicted hacker) Rui Pinto. UEFA conducted an investigation, and in 2020 found the club guilty, though the punishments (a two-year ban from European competitions and a €30m fine) were watered down on appeal. Meanwhile, Manchester City kept on winning.

“There was wide recognition that Manchester City had gotten away with it by dragging out the process,” Wilson tells me – the Court of Arbitration for Sport found the club showed a “blatant disregard” to Uefa’s investigation. “There was a sense then that football could not really handle situations like these,” Wilson says.Then, last month, the Premier League announcement came: Manchester City was guilty of 114 charges. It’s understood these offences correlate to information already in the public domain: that Manchester City inflated the value of sponsorship deals to channel extra cash into the club; that secret payments were made to senior club figures and player agents. These were a contravention of financial rules, and the club “made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate” Premier League investigations.
The club has maintained its innocence, and intends to appeal.

Even allowing time for Manchester City to appeal, a sanction decision is expected around Christmas. Fines, point-docking, transfer bans, suspension and expulsion are all being discussed, though Premier League rules dictate there’s no limit to the penalties that could be dished out. The sheer scale of the rule-breaking means there’s little precedent for comparison. Everton were docked six points for a £20 million rule breach. Apply the same metrics, and Manchester City would lose hundreds. Knocking that much off their tally in a single season is “functionally identical” to a much softer sentence, says Wilson. (Points reset every season, and last year, league-toppers Arsenal finished on just 85.)

“It leads to the conclusion that expulsion from the Premier League might be the only logical outcome,” says Wilson. He’d also like them stripped of their titles, and to see an investigation launched immediately into the club’s finances from 2018 until now.

Expulsion would be complicated. The complex structure of English football means if Manchester City did get booted out of the Premier League, there’s no guarantee the club would find a place in a lower league. And, even if it’s recommended by the panel, Premier League clubs would need to vote it through on a two-thirds majority. “That vote is unpredictable, as some club owners have business ties in Abu Dhabi or fear setting a precedent where clubs can vote out rivals,” says Wilson.
How worried should Man City be?

Off the pitch, there’s the prospect of civil litigation lingering too: Liverpool, Arsenal, Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur each submitted formal legal notices before a September 2024 deadline, which reserves them the right to claim compensation for losses caused by City’s rule breaches. When Everton breached financial rules in the 2021/22 season Burnley successfully claimed close to £40m from the Merseyside club. The sums at stake in this instance could be eye-watering. Plus there’s the prospect of possible criminal proceedings. Tom Forster KC, a financial crime barrister, suggested that Manchester City “has a great deal to be worried about on this front”.

Then there’s the political fallout, which is still taking shape. Andy Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester through this period, a time during which Abu Dhabi made serious investments in the city. “That can be viewed either as benevolent community building or as a calculated investment, expecting returns and local influence,” says Wilson. Either way, it’s not ideal for the new prime minister.

Plus, Burnham’s initial response to the judgment raised eyebrows, saying he’d be “really concerned” if the owners were forced to sell. “His skepticism of the charges sounded like comments from a fan on a message board rather than a measured politician,” says Wilson. Clarifications from Number 10 soon followed, and Burnham committed to publishing details of his dealings with Manchester City. Yesterday, he requested a “manual trawl” of records from his time as Greater Manchester Mayor, after two hospitality dinners with Manchester City’s chair were found to be absent from the combined authority’s digital register.
What does this mean for English football?

The ramifications for English football are clear. The Premier League faces a massive problem: the success of its top side is built on foul play. And not just between 2009 and 2018, Wilson reckons. “Even if we assume City complied cleanly after the leaks emerged, their success since remains predicated on that unfair advantage. That’s a lot of titles – and a lot of prize money – won under compromised conditions.

As it stands, this is “hugely damaging” to the Premier League’s reputation and fan trust, Wilson says. Football is the UK’s most popular sport, and is worth billions to the economy. If faith is lost in the sport, that’s a real problem. On the other hand, football is just a ballgame without the drama, spectacle and narrative – to which this debacle adds plenty. Especially, Wilson says, “if the outcome demonstrates that the Premier League is willing to enforce its regulations against even its most dominant team.”

But there’s a story much bigger than football here. Manchester City (and Saudi Arabia’s Newcastle United for that matter) aren’t the only British institutions quasi-owned by foreign governments. Qatar, Saudi and China own the bulk of Heathrow Airport; through state-owned EDF, France claims significant chunks of UK energy infrastructure. Royal Mail, meanwhile, is owned by a Czech billionaire; more than 70% of the English water industry is in foreign ownership.

“This case illustrates the extent of foreign state influence over major British institutions,” says Wilson, “tracing back to New Labour policies that encouraged foreign state investment without sufficient safeguards against geopolitical manipulation.” But, if the Premier League holds course, its response could be just as symbolic. “In a broader societal landscape where massive wealth often overrides accountability, this would represent a major British institution taking a stand to enforce rule of law and regulatory compliance.”
